svg.title: Passkey sign-in: Supabase proof of concept and other stacks
svg.desc: Top: the three steps (admin adds a person, person sets up a passkey, person signs in) and what the phone, the app server, Supabase Auth and the Supabase database each do. Bottom: a table of the same five jobs done with Supabase, with your own server and a WebAuthn library, and with a managed auth service. Then the five ideas that stay the same on any stack.
svg.text: Passkey sign-in: how the proof of concept works, and how to build it on another stack
Top: what we built (Next.js and Supabase). Bottom: the same jobs on a stack of your own.
A
What we built
The three steps, and who does what in each
Phone or browser
The person's own device
Admin types a name and an email, then
sends the link by hand.
Member opens the link and presses
Continue. The phone makes the key after a
face or fingerprint. The key never leaves
the phone.
Member presses Sign in with a passkey. The
phone signs a challenge. No email typed.
App server
Next.js on Vercel. Holds the secrets
Checks the admin. Makes a one-time link: a
random 256-bit token, only its hash is
kept, 15 minutes.
Spends the link when Continue is pressed
(opening it spends nothing). Hands over a
short setup session.
On every page: verifies the token and
requires that it was made by a passkey.
Anything else is refused.
Supabase Auth
Hosted service. Passkeys turned on
Creates the account with a random password
nobody sees.
Stores the public key when
registerPasskey() runs in the browser.
Checks the signature and issues the
session token, marked amr = passkey.
Supabase database
No table access. 8 checked functions
Stores the member and the hash of the
link.
Spends the link in one atomic update:
right hash, unused, not expired.
Says who the member is, reading the id
from the token, never from a form field.
calls
calls
calls
The one rule, checked on every page:
did this person get in with a passkey? A setup link does not count. A password does not count.
B
The same jobs on another stack
Five jobs, whatever you build on
What we used: Supabase
Your own server and a WebAuthn library
A managed auth service
Add the member and send the
first link
createUser with a random password, then generateLink and
verifyOtp to open a short setup session. The link itself is our
own token.
Your admin page and a table of one-time tokens (hash only,
expiry, used flag). No account session is needed: the server
can issue the registration challenge directly.
Use the provider's invite or enrolment feature, or keep the
same own-token link in front of it.
Keep the account and the
public key
Supabase Auth holds the user and the passkey's public key. Our
own tables hold the member and the link hash.
Two tables you own: users, and credentials (credential id,
public key, counter, transports). Works in Postgres, MySQL or
MongoDB.
The provider holds both. You keep your own member list and
roles.
Create the passkey (once)
registerPasskey() runs in the browser. Supabase checks the
reply and stores the key.
The server makes a challenge and checks the phone's reply with
a library, for example SimpleWebAuthn (Node), py_webauthn
(Python), Spring Security 6.4+ (Java), Fido2NetLib (.NET),
go-webauthn (Go), webauthn-ruby (Rails), webauthn-framework
(PHP).
Switch passkeys on in the provider (for example Auth0, AWS
Cognito, Keycloak, Clerk or Hanko) and call its SDK.
Sign in with the passkey
(every time)
signInWithPasskey(). No email typed. Supabase checks the
signature and issues the session.
Same library, sign-in half. Use discoverable credentials so no
email is typed, then issue your own session or JWT.
A hosted login page or an SDK call. The provider issues the
token.
Prove it was a passkey, on
every page
The token's amr claim lists passkey. getClaims() verifies the
token on the server and the app checks amr.
Your session records method = passkey at sign-in. Check it on
the server on every request, and do not trust a client-side
object.
Look for a sign-in-method claim in the token. Names differ by
provider, so confirm one exists before you rely on it.
Same on every stack, because none of it is Supabase
The setup link is a random token, stored only as a keyed hash, good for one use and 15 minutes.
Opening the link spends nothing. Pressing Continue spends it, so chat previews cannot burn it.
The server checks the sign-in method on every page. Hiding a page is not the check.
Passkeys belong to the site address (the relying-party ID). Pick the final domain before anyone enrols.
Tell people to open links in Safari or Chrome, not inside a chat or mail app.
Proof of concept, built with AI assistance. The Supabase half is checked against the code (handover/build.py).
Library and service names in column 2 and 3 are from general knowledge and were not tested here: confirm current versions and passkey support before choosing. Details: carry-over.md, known-gaps.md.
